p.src: When a Discrete Label Becomes Continuous

u.src: When a Discrete Label Becomes Continuous
en: When a Discrete Label Becomes Continuous

p.src: Begin with an observable whose possible values are labeled by integers $n=1,2,\ldots$. Its probabilities obey $\sum_n P(n)=1,$ and the corresponding basis vectors may be chosen orthonormally: $\braket m n=\delta_{mn}.$ The Kronecker delta is one when its two labels agree and zero otherwise. It can equally well be regarded as a function of the difference $m-n$.

p.src:
Let the measured quantity now be the position $x$ of a particle on a line. For an ordinary continuous distribution, a single point has zero probability. The useful object is therefore a probability density $\rho(x)$. The probability of finding the particle in a short interval is $\begin{aligned}
  \operatorname{Prob}\!\left(x_1\leq x\leq x_2\right)
  &=\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\rho(x)\,dx,\\
  \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\rho(x)\,dx&=1.
  \end{aligned}$ Thus sums become integrals, and probability masses become densities.

p.src: The Dirac Delta

u.src: The Dirac Delta
en: The Dirac Delta

p.src:
The continuum analogue of the Kronecker delta is the Dirac delta distribution. Its informal picture is an infinitely narrow spike at $x=y$, zero away from that point, with unit area: $\delta(x-y)=0\quad (x\neq y),
  \qquad
  \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(x-y)\,dx=1.$ No ordinary function has these properties. The precise definition is its action on a sufficiently regular test function: $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(x-y)f(x)\,dx=f(y).$ The delta is therefore best understood as a distribution under an integral, not as a function with a literal infinite value.

p.src:
A useful approximation makes the spike picture explicit. Let $\delta_\epsilon(x-y)$ be a rectangle of width $\epsilon$ and height $1/\epsilon$, centered at $y$. Its area is one, and for continuous $f$, $\int \delta_\epsilon(x-y)f(x)\,dx
    \longrightarrow f(y)
  \qquad (\epsilon\to0).$ The unit area must not be confused with a unit Hilbert-space norm: $\int\left|\delta_\epsilon\right|^{2}dx=1/\epsilon$ diverges in the limit.

p.src: The Position Amplitude and Born Density

u.src: The Position Amplitude and Born Density
en: The Position Amplitude and Born Density

p.src:
The abstract probability rule has not changed. In the discrete case, $\left|\braket n\psi\right|^{2}$ is the probability for the outcome $n$. In the continuous case, $\rho(y)=\left|\braket y\psi\right|^{2}$ is the probability density at $y$. To see what this means in the position representation, write $\psi(x):=\braket x\psi.$ The wavefunction of the generalized position state $\ket y$ is $\braket x y=\delta(x-y)$. Hence $\begin{aligned}
  \braket y\psi
    &=\int dx\,\braket yx\braket x\psi \\
    &=\int dx\,\delta(x-y)\psi(x)
      =\psi(y).
  \end{aligned}$ Born’s rule is therefore $\begin{aligned}
  \rho(y)&=\left|\psi(y)\right|^{2},\\
  \operatorname{Prob}(y\in[a,b])
  &=\int_a^b\left|\psi(y)\right|^{2}\,dy.
  \end{aligned}$

p.src: A Lattice Explains Continuum Normalization

u.src: A Lattice Explains Continuum Normalization
en: A Lattice Explains Continuum Normalization

p.src:
The divergent self-overlap of $\ket x$ becomes transparent if the line is temporarily replaced by a lattice with spacing $a$. Let $x_n=na$, and let $\ket n$ be ordinary normalized site states: $\braket n m=\delta_{nm},
  \qquad
  \sum_n\ket n\bra n=\mathbf 1.$ Define continuum-normalized states at the lattice points by $\ket{x_n}:=\frac{1}{\sqrt a}\ket n.$ Their overlap and completeness relations are $\braket{x_n}{x_m}=\frac{\delta_{nm}}{a},
  \qquad
  \sum_n a\,\ket{x_n}\bra{x_n}=\mathbf 1.$ As $a\to0$, the sum $\sum_n a$ becomes an integral, while $\delta_{nm}/a$ becomes $\delta(x-y)$. The height $1/a$ and width $a$ again give unit area.

p.src: Now constrain the particle to a circle of radius $R$. Cutting the circle at one point turns it into the interval $0\leq x<2\pi R,$ but the two ends represent the same physical point. The wavefunction must therefore satisfy $\psi(x+2\pi R)=\psi(x).$ Periodic functions form a complex vector space: scalar multiples and sums of periodic functions are still periodic.

p.src: Periodicity Quantizes Momentum

u.src: Periodicity Quantizes Momentum
en: Periodicity Quantizes Momentum

p.src:
The normalized plane wave is not automatically an allowed state. It must also obey the periodic boundary condition: $\begin{aligned}
  e^{ip(x+2\pi R)/\hbar}&=e^{ipx/\hbar},\\
  e^{i2\pi Rp/\hbar}&=1.\end{aligned}$ The phase gained in one circuit must be an integer multiple of $2\pi$: $\frac{2\pi Rp}{\hbar}=2\pi n,
  \qquad n\in\mathbb Z.$ Thus $p_n=\frac{n\hbar}{R},
  \qquad
  \psi_n(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi R}}e^{inx/R}.$

u.src: Compatibility and Common Eigenstates
en: Compatibility and Common Eigenstates

p.src: A classical particle may be assigned a position and a momentum at the same instant. Quantum mechanically, a position eigenstate is localized like a delta distribution, whereas a momentum eigenstate is a plane wave with uniform position density. These states cannot be the same.

p.src:
The algebraic question is whether two Hermitian operators $\hat A$ and $\hat B$ possess a complete common eigenbasis. If $\hat A\ket n=a_n\ket n,
  \qquad
  \hat B\ket n=b_n\ket n,$ then $\hat A\hat B\ket n=a_nb_n\ket n
  =\hat B\hat A\ket n.$ Define the commutator $:=\hat A\hat B-\hat B\hat A.$ Compatible observables commute. Conversely, commuting Hermitian matrices can be simultaneously diagonalized, including within degenerate eigenspaces. For unbounded operators, the same statement requires compatible domains and the corresponding spectral conditions; those analytic details are suppressed here.

p.src: The Canonical Commutator

u.src: The Canonical Commutator
en: The Canonical Commutator

p.src:
For position and momentum, $(\hat x\psi)(x)=x\psi(x),
  \qquad
  (\hat p\psi)(x)=-i\hbar\psi'(x).$ Apply their commutator to an arbitrary differentiable wavefunction: $\begin{aligned}
\psi
    &=x\left(-i\hbar\frac{d\psi}{dx}\right)
      +i\hbar\frac{d}{dx}\bigl(x\psi\bigr)\\
    &=-i\hbar x\psi'
      +i\hbar\bigl(\psi+x\psi'\bigr)\\
    &=i\hbar\psi.\end{aligned}$ Since this holds for every state in the common domain, $=i\hbar\,\mathbf 1.$

p.src:
The two-slit experiment turns the linear structure of states into a visible probability pattern. An incoming particle meets a barrier with two small openings, and a screen records the position $y$ at which it arrives. With only one opening available, the outgoing wave spreads. In three dimensions a schematic far-field contribution has the form $\psi(r)\sim\frac{e^{ikr}}{r},
  \qquad
  r=\sqrt{\ell^2+y^2},$ where $\ell$ is the distance from aperture to screen. Over a small region of the screen it may be approximated by a local plane wave.

p.src:
Now open both holes. Let $\psi_1(y)$ and $\psi_2(y)$ be the amplitudes associated with the two alternatives. The state-space rule is $\psi(y)=\psi_1(y)+\psi_2(y),$ not the addition of the separate probabilities. Locally, suppressing slowly varying envelopes and temporarily setting $\hbar=1$, write $\psi_1=e^{ipy},
  \qquad
  \psi_2=e^{iqy}.$ Then $\begin{aligned}
  \left|\psi_1+\psi_2\right|^{2}
    &=(e^{ipy}+e^{iqy})(e^{-ipy}+e^{-iqy})\\
    &=2+e^{i(p-q)y}+e^{-i(p-q)y}\\
    &=2+2\cos\bigl((p-q)y\bigr).
  \end{aligned}$ The cross terms retain the relative phase. They create alternating bright and dark fringes even though either local plane wave separately has constant magnitude.

p.src: In the far field, if the slit separation is $d$, the path difference at angle $\theta$ is approximately $d\sin\theta$. For wavelength $\lambda=2\pi/k$, adjacent bright fringes satisfy $d\sin\theta_m=m\lambda.$ At small angles, $y\approx\ell\theta$, so $\Delta y\approx\frac{\lambda\ell}{d}.$ Moving the holes farther apart makes the fringes closer; moving them together spreads the fringes apart.

p.src: Phase Gradients and Elastic Deflection

u.src: Phase Gradients and Elastic Deflection
en: Phase Gradients and Elastic Deflection

p.src: For a wave of the form $e^{i\phi(y)}$, the local vertical momentum is the phase gradient $p_y(y)=\hbar\frac{d\phi}{dy}.$ Near the central axis the distance $r=\sqrt{\ell^2+y^2}$ changes slowly with $y$, so the vertical phase gradient is small. Farther from the axis, the wave has a larger vertical momentum component. This does not require an increase in kinetic energy. In an elastic scattering picture, the magnitude of the momentum remains fixed: $p_x^2+p_y^2=p^2.$ An increase in $\left|p_y\right|$ is accompanied by a decrease in $\left|p_x\right|$; the momentum vector changes direction rather than length.

p.src: The wavefunction describes both alternatives, but each detection event is a localized spot. Send one electron at a time and the screen records one spot at a time. Repeat the preparation many times and the accumulated spots approach the density $\left|\psi_1+\psi_2\right|^{2}$. The density cannot be negative because it is an absolute square, but it can vanish where the two amplitudes cancel.

p.src: A finite aperture can also diffract by itself. Different points across a sharp opening contribute different phases, so a single-slit envelope may contain maxima and minima of its own. This is distinct from the finer two-slit modulation, although a real experiment displays both at once.

p.src: Visibility, Wavelength, and Idealization

u.src: Visibility, Wavelength, and Idealization
en: Visibility, Wavelength, and Idealization

p.src:
Exact dark fringes require coherent contributions of equal magnitude. If the two apertures have unequal amplitudes $A_1$ and $A_2$, then $I(y)=\left|A_1\right|^{2}+\left|A_2\right|^{2}
       +2\left|A_1A_2\right|\cos\Delta\phi(y).$ The minimum is $(\left|A_1\right|-\left|A_2\right|)^2$, so unequal illumination fills in the dark fringes. Noise, finite source coherence, detector resolution, and imperfect geometry do the same. Under ideal conditions the minima can nevertheless be extremely dark.

p.src: Passing through a sufficiently small opening prepares an approximate outgoing state centered at that opening. In this limited sense the later pattern can become insensitive to many details of the source. Coherence still matters: the source and apparatus must not carry distinguishable which-path information.

en: Reuse Is Not Reversal

p.src: The final question separates two ideas that are easy to confuse. One may collect an electron, prepare it again, and repeat the experiment with that same particle; repeated trials do not require newly created electrons. Reversing an entire detected event is a different matter. The screen and all other correlated degrees of freedom would have to be included in the reversal.

p.src: That is where the calculation properly stops. The kinematics has supplied continuous bases, delta normalization, quantized momentum on a circle, noncommuting position and momentum, and interference from added amplitudes. The next step is dynamics: a Hamiltonian must say how these states evolve in time.
